specStatements.text: There is an observed increase in the wavelength of light from most distant galaxies. The further away the galaxies, the faster they are moving and the bigger the observed increase in wavelength. This effect is called red-shift.
The observed red-shift provides evidence that space itself (the universe) is expanding and supports the Big Bang theory.
The Big Bang theory suggests that the universe began from a very small region that was extremely hot and dense.
Since 1998 onwards, observations of supernovae suggest that distant galaxies are receding ever faster.
Students should be able to explain:
• qualitatively the red-shift of light from galaxies that are receding
• that the change of each galaxy’s speed with distance is evidence of an expanding universe
• how red-shift provides evidence for the Big Bang model
• how scientists are able to use observations to arrive at theories such as the Big Bang theory
• that there is still much about the universe that is not understood, for example dark mass and dark energy.

scopeNotes.statement: • qualitatively the red-shift of light from galaxies that are receding
scopeNotes.howHonoured: The specification asks for a qualitative explanation only, so no numerical treatment of red-shift appears in this content. There is no equation relating change in wavelength to speed of recession, no Hubble relationship of the form speed = constant x distance, and no calculation of a galaxy's speed, of its distance, or of the age of the universe, from a wavelength shift. Every item asks the student to compare shifts as bigger or smaller and to state the matching conclusion about speed and distance in words.

scopeNotes.statement: There is an observed increase in the wavelength of light from most distant galaxies.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: The specification says most distant galaxies, not all galaxies, and this content keeps that wording. No item states or implies that every object in the sky shows an increased wavelength. Blue-shift, which the specification does not name, is never required knowledge; it appears only as the wrong direction of shift in a single distractor, where the student needs nothing beyond the specification's own statement that the observed change is an increase in wavelength.

concepts.definition: The observed increase in the wavelength of light from most distant galaxies. The same light, when produced on Earth, has a shorter wavelength, so features in the galaxy's spectrum are found nearer the red end. This effect is called red-shift.
The distance from one wave crest to the next. Visible light of longer wavelength lies towards the red end of the spectrum, so an increase in wavelength moves a spectral feature towards the red end.
Moving away from the observer. A galaxy that is receding shows an increase in the wavelength of its light, and the faster it recedes the bigger that increase is.

The way red-shift is observed. The pattern of lines produced by a known element on Earth is compared with the same pattern in the light from a galaxy; for a red-shifted galaxy the whole pattern sits at longer wavelengths.

The further away the galaxies, the faster they are moving and the bigger the observed increase in wavelength. A bigger red-shift therefore means both a greater speed of recession and a greater distance.

The picture in which space itself grows, carrying the galaxies apart, rather than galaxies travelling out through a space that was already there. The change of each galaxy's speed with distance is evidence for it.
The theory that the universe began from a very small region that was extremely hot and dense. The observed red-shift supports it, because an expanding universe must once have been very much smaller.

Scientists make observations, such as the red-shift of light from distant galaxies, and put forward a theory that explains them. The theory is then tested against further observations and may be developed or replaced.
Observations of supernovae made since 1998 onwards. They suggest that distant galaxies are receding ever faster, which changed what scientists say about how the universe is expanding.
Matter whose presence is inferred from its effects but which is not understood. The specification gives it as an example of how much about the universe is still not understood.
The name given to whatever is causing distant galaxies to recede ever faster. Like dark mass, it is given in the specification as an example of what is still not understood.

misconceptions.question: A galaxy shows a large red-shift. Does it look red?
misconceptions.correct: No. Red-shift means the wavelength of its light has increased, so lines in its spectrum sit nearer the red end than the laboratory lines do.
misconceptions.misconception: Red-shift means the galaxy has turned red, so a red-shifted galaxy looks red and a galaxy that does not look red is not red-shifted.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The name contains a colour, and the only shift a student has met before is a change of colour, so the term is read as a description of appearance.
misconceptions.correction: The evidence is the position of lines in a spectrum, not the overall colour. The whole pattern from a known element is found at longer wavelengths than the laboratory pattern, and that movement towards the red end is what the word names.

misconceptions.question: Does red-shift mean the wavelength of the light gets shorter?
misconceptions.correct: No. Red-shift is an observed increase in the wavelength of light from most distant galaxies.
misconceptions.misconception: Red-shift squashes the light into shorter wavelengths, because the galaxy is racing away and the waves are compressed behind it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students remember that recession changes the wave but picture the waves being bunched up rather than stretched out, and shift is remembered without its direction.
misconceptions.correction: A receding source stretches the waves reaching the observer, so the wavelength increases. The specification defines red-shift as an observed increase in wavelength, and longer wavelength lies towards the red end.

misconceptions.question: Is red-shift caused by dust reddening the light on its journey?
misconceptions.correct: No. Red-shift is an increase in wavelength linked to the recession of the galaxy, not a change caused by material along the path.
misconceptions.misconception: The light passes through dust and loses energy on the way, which reddens it in the way a sunset is reddened.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Reddening by the atmosphere is a familiar everyday effect, and it offers a mechanism that seems to explain the colour word in the term.
misconceptions.correction: Reddening dims light without moving spectral lines. In red-shift the entire pattern of lines is displaced to longer wavelengths, and the size of that displacement grows with the distance and speed of the galaxy.

misconceptions.question: Does an increase in wavelength mean the galaxy is coming towards us?
misconceptions.correct: No. An observed increase in wavelength means the galaxy is receding, that is, moving away from us.
misconceptions.misconception: A galaxy coming towards us pushes its waves out in front of it and stretches them, so a longer wavelength means approach.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The idea of waves being pushed ahead of a moving source is half remembered, and the pushing is imagined as stretching rather than compressing.
misconceptions.correction: Waves ahead of an approaching source are compressed, giving a shorter wavelength. The specification links the observed increase in wavelength to galaxies that are receding.

misconceptions.question: Does light slow down over such a long journey, giving a longer wavelength?
misconceptions.correct: No. The increase in wavelength is due to the recession of the galaxy, not to the light losing speed.
misconceptions.misconception: Light gets tired over an enormous journey and slows down, and slower light must have a longer wavelength when it arrives.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Everyday moving objects slow down over long distances, and the idea is carried across to light without checking it.
misconceptions.correction: Light travels at the same speed through space however far it goes. What changes is the wavelength, and it changes because the source is receding.

misconceptions.question: Does a bigger red-shift mean a bigger or brighter galaxy?
misconceptions.correct: No. A bigger observed increase in wavelength means the galaxy is moving faster and is further away.
misconceptions.misconception: A large bright galaxy sends more light and so gives a bigger red-shift, so red-shift is really a measure of the size of the galaxy.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Bigger is taken to mean bigger in every sense, and the size of an effect is attached to the size of the object producing it.
misconceptions.correction: Red-shift is measured from the position of spectral lines, which does not depend on how big or bright the source is. The specification links a bigger observed increase in wavelength to greater speed and greater distance.

misconceptions.question: Which galaxies are moving fastest, the nearest or the most distant?
misconceptions.correct: The most distant. The further away the galaxies, the faster they are moving.
misconceptions.misconception: The nearer galaxies must be the fast ones, because things slow down the further they travel, so the distant ones have lost speed.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Everyday experience of objects slowing down as they travel is applied to galaxies, which reverses the relationship the specification gives.
misconceptions.correction: The specification states the opposite: the further away the galaxies, the faster they are moving and the bigger the observed increase in wavelength. Speed rises with distance rather than falling.

misconceptions.question: Every distant galaxy is receding from us. Are we at the centre of the universe?
misconceptions.correct: No. Any observer anywhere would see the same thing, because space itself is expanding everywhere.
misconceptions.misconception: If everything moves away from us in every direction then we must be standing at the centre of the expansion.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The only familiar way for things to move away in all directions is to be at the middle of an explosion, so a centre is assumed.
misconceptions.correction: When space itself stretches, the distance between every pair of galaxies grows, so any observer sees all the others receding and sees the more distant ones receding faster. No observation singles out a centre.

misconceptions.question: Did the Big Bang throw matter outwards into space that was already there?
misconceptions.correct: No. The evidence is that space itself, the universe, is expanding, rather than that galaxies travel out through a fixed space.
misconceptions.misconception: The galaxies were thrown outwards by a huge explosion and are flying away through empty space that was already sitting there.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word bang brings a firework or a bomb to mind, and every explosion a student has seen happens inside a room or a sky that already exists.
misconceptions.correction: The observed red-shift is evidence that space itself is expanding, so the galaxies are carried apart by the growth of space rather than travelling through a pre-existing space.

misconceptions.question: Was the Big Bang an enormous star exploding?
misconceptions.correct: No. The Big Bang theory suggests the universe began from a very small region that was extremely hot and dense.
misconceptions.misconception: The Big Bang was a giant star that blew up, in the same way that a supernova is an exploding star.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Supernovae appear in the same section of the specification, and both are described with the word explosion, so the two are merged.
misconceptions.correction: A supernova is one star exploding within a universe that already exists. The Big Bang theory describes the beginning of the universe itself, from a very small, extremely hot and dense region.

misconceptions.question: What did observations of supernovae made since 1998 onwards suggest?
misconceptions.correct: That distant galaxies are receding ever faster.
misconceptions.misconception: The observations showed that the expansion is running out of energy, so distant galaxies are gradually slowing down.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Thrown objects always slow down, so an expansion that started long ago is expected to be losing speed by now.
misconceptions.correction: The specification states the opposite: since 1998 onwards, observations of supernovae suggest that distant galaxies are receding ever faster.

misconceptions.question: Did the Big Bang theory come from the supernova observations made since 1998?
misconceptions.correct: No. The theory was already established; the supernova observations refined what scientists say about how the expansion is changing.
misconceptions.misconception: The Big Bang theory came from the 1998 supernova observations, since those are the observations the specification names.
misconceptions.whyItArises: It is the only date given in the section, so it is attached to the biggest idea in the section.
misconceptions.correction: Red-shift observations are the evidence that supports the Big Bang theory. The supernova observations made since 1998 onwards added the later finding that distant galaxies are receding ever faster.

misconceptions.question: Red-shift supports the Big Bang theory. Does that make the theory a proven fact?
misconceptions.correct: No. It is a theory supported by evidence, and it can be developed or changed when new observations are made.
misconceptions.misconception: Red-shift proves the Big Bang, so the theory is now a fact and no new evidence could ever alter it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Proof is treated as the goal of science, so strong supporting evidence is read as closing the question for good.
misconceptions.correction: Scientists use observations to arrive at theories, and those theories are tested against further observations. The supernova observations made since 1998 onwards changed what is said about the expansion, which shows that a theory can still develop.

misconceptions.question: Nobody witnessed the beginning of the universe. Does that make the Big Bang untestable?
misconceptions.correct: No. A theory is tested by whether its consequences match what is observed now, such as the red-shift of light from distant galaxies.
misconceptions.misconception: The Big Bang is just somebody's guess about the past, because nobody was there to see it and so it cannot be tested.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Testing is imagined as watching an event happen, so an event in the distant past seems to be beyond the reach of evidence.
misconceptions.correction: A theory is tested by the observations it leads us to expect. The Big Bang model accounts for the observed red-shift of light from most distant galaxies, and further observations continue to test and develop it.

misconceptions.question: Are dark mass and dark energy two names for the same thing?
misconceptions.correct: No. They are given in the specification as two separate examples of what is still not understood about the universe.
misconceptions.misconception: Dark mass and dark energy both just mean the invisible stuff out in space, so the two terms can be swapped freely.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both terms begin with the same word and both refer to something that cannot be seen, so they are collapsed into one idea.
misconceptions.correction: Dark mass concerns matter that is not seen directly, while dark energy is the name attached to the ever faster recession of distant galaxies. The specification lists them as two examples of what is not understood.

misconceptions.question: Are dark mass and dark energy explained parts of the Big Bang theory?
misconceptions.correct: No. The specification gives them as examples of how much about the universe is still not understood.
misconceptions.misconception: Dark mass and dark energy are fully explained parts of the theory, and scientists already know what they are made of.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Anything that has a name and appears in a specification is assumed to be a settled piece of knowledge.
misconceptions.correction: The specification states that there is still much about the universe that is not understood, for example dark mass and dark energy. Naming something is not the same as explaining it.

mcqs.stem: Light from a distant galaxy is compared with light from the same element produced in a laboratory on Earth. What is observed about the light from the galaxy?

options.text: Its wavelength is longer than the laboratory value
options.rationale: Red-shift is an observed increase in the wavelength of light from most distant galaxies, so the galaxy's light arrives with a longer wavelength than the same light produced on Earth.

options.text: Its wavelength is shorter than the value on Earth
options.rationale: A student who remembers that a shift happens but not its direction chooses the opposite change.

options.text: It looks red instead of its normal colour
options.rationale: The colour word in red-shift is read as a description of how the galaxy appears.

options.text: It has been reddened by dust on the way here
options.rationale: Sunsets are reddened by the atmosphere, so dust is offered as the cause of the shift.

mcqs.stem: The light from galaxy B shows a bigger observed increase in wavelength than the light from galaxy A. What can be concluded about galaxy B?

options.text: It is moving faster, so it must be closer to us
options.rationale: Treats a bigger red-shift as faster and, inverting distance, judges the faster galaxy to be nearer.

options.text: It is further away than A and is moving faster
options.rationale: The specification states that the further away the galaxies, the faster they are moving and the bigger the observed increase in wavelength.

options.text: It is nearer than A and is moving more slowly
options.rationale: A student who thinks moving objects slow down as they travel expects the fast ones to be close by.

options.text: It is a larger and brighter galaxy than A
options.rationale: The size of the shift is confused with the size or brightness of the galaxy producing it.

mcqs.stem: The light from most distant galaxies shows red-shift. What does this observation provide evidence for?

options.text: That the galaxies fly out through existing space
options.rationale: Expansion of space is replaced by ordinary motion through a fixed, pre-existing space.

options.text: That the Earth sits at the centre of the universe
options.rationale: Recession seen in every direction is read as proof that we occupy a special central place.

options.text: That space itself, the universe, is expanding
options.rationale: The specification states that the observed red-shift provides evidence that space itself (the universe) is expanding.

options.text: That the distant galaxies are slowing down
options.rationale: Red-shift is treated as a measure of how quickly a galaxy is losing speed.

mcqs.stem: According to the Big Bang theory, what was the universe like at the very beginning?

options.text: A giant star that collapsed and then blew apart
options.rationale: Imagines the Big Bang as an exploding star, a supernova collapsing then blowing apart.

options.text: A single giant star that exploded out into space
options.rationale: The word bang suggests an exploding star, so the Big Bang is pictured as a supernova.

options.text: A large empty space that matter exploded into
options.rationale: The beginning is imagined as an explosion inside a space that was already sitting there.

options.text: A very small region, extremely hot and dense
options.rationale: The specification states that the Big Bang theory suggests the universe began from a very small region that was extremely hot and dense.

mcqs.stem: What do observations of supernovae made since 1998 onwards suggest about distant galaxies?

options.text: They are gradually slowing as they recede
options.rationale: Everyday moving objects slow down, so the expansion is assumed to be running down too.

options.text: They are receding ever faster as time goes on
options.rationale: The specification states that since 1998 onwards, observations of supernovae suggest that distant galaxies are receding ever faster.

options.text: They will slow to a stop and then fall back
options.rationale: Thinks the expansion is running out of energy, so galaxies slow, stop and fall back.

options.text: The nearest of them are receding fastest
options.rationale: The relationship between distance and speed is inverted, so nearby galaxies are made the fast ones.

mcqs.stem: Every distant galaxy is observed to be receding, and the further away a galaxy is the faster it recedes. Why is this evidence that the universe is expanding?

options.text: Because the galaxies were thrown outwards through space
options.rationale: Expansion of space is replaced by galaxies flying through a space that already existed.

options.text: Because the Earth must be at the centre of it all
options.rationale: Seeing recession in every direction is taken as evidence of a central position.

options.text: Because space between all the galaxies is stretching
options.rationale: The change of each galaxy's speed with distance is what the specification names as evidence of an expanding universe: space itself grows, so more distant galaxies separate from us faster.

options.text: Because nearer galaxies are moving away faster
options.rationale: Inverts the distance-speed relation, wrongly claiming the nearer galaxies recede fastest.

mcqs.stem: How does the observed red-shift provide evidence for the Big Bang model?

options.text: The stretched light is left over from the original explosion
options.rationale: The red-shifted light itself is mistaken for debris from a single past explosion.

options.text: It proves the Big Bang, so the theory can never be changed
options.rationale: Supporting evidence is treated as final proof rather than as support for a model.

options.text: The red colour shows the early universe was very hot
options.rationale: The colour word is linked to heat, so red-shift is read as a temperature measurement.

options.text: An expanding universe must once have been small and dense
options.rationale: Red-shift shows the universe is expanding; running that expansion backwards leads to the very small, extremely hot and dense beginning the Big Bang theory suggests.

mcqs.stem: Which statement best describes how scientists were able to use observations to arrive at the Big Bang theory?

options.text: A model was proposed to explain what was observed
options.rationale: Scientists build a theory that accounts for the observations, such as red-shift, and keep testing that theory against further observations.

options.text: Red-shift observations proved the theory to be true
options.rationale: Treats red-shift as absolute proof, so the observations are said to prove the theory true.

options.text: Nobody saw the beginning, so the theory is untestable
options.rationale: A theory about the past is assumed to be untestable because the event was not witnessed.

options.text: The theory came from the 1998 supernova observations
options.rationale: The only date named in the specification is attached to the origin of the whole theory.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about dark mass and dark energy matches what the specification says?

options.text: They are fully explained by the Big Bang theory
options.rationale: Anything named in a theory is assumed to be a settled, explained part of it.

options.text: They both name the same invisible material
options.rationale: Both terms contain the word dark, so they are treated as interchangeable.

options.text: They are examples of what is still not understood
options.rationale: The specification states that there is still much about the universe that is not understood, for example dark mass and dark energy.

options.text: The 1998 supernova results predicted them both
options.rationale: Over-credits the 1998 supernova observations, wrongly making them the source of dark mass and dark energy.

mcqs.stem: The pattern of lines in the spectrum of a distant galaxy is compared with the pattern produced by the same element on Earth. What is observed?

options.text: The lines are shifted towards the blue end
options.rationale: The direction of the shift is reversed, which would indicate approach rather than recession.

options.text: The whole galaxy appears red rather than white
options.rationale: The evidence is looked for in the galaxy's overall colour instead of in the line positions.

options.text: The lines are brighter and further apart
options.rationale: The shift is confused with a change in the brightness of the source.

options.text: The lines are all shifted towards the red end
options.rationale: Red-shift is seen as the whole pattern of lines from a known element appearing at longer wavelengths than the laboratory pattern.

mcqs.stem: Light from galaxies X, Y and Z is examined. X shows a small increase in wavelength, Y a medium increase and Z a large increase. Which galaxy is furthest away?

options.text: Z, because it shows the biggest increase
options.rationale: The bigger the observed increase in wavelength, the faster the galaxy is moving and the further away it is, so Z is the most distant of the three.

options.text: X, because it shows the smallest increase
options.rationale: The relationship is inverted, so the smallest shift is read as the greatest distance.

options.text: Y, because its shift shows a medium-sized galaxy
options.rationale: Treats red-shift as a measure of galaxy size, so a medium shift means a medium galaxy.

options.text: X, because it has lost the most speed
options.rationale: Believes distant galaxies lose speed, so the smallest shift (X) is taken as the furthest.

mcqs.stem: Observations of supernovae made since 1998 onwards changed what scientists say about the expansion of the universe. What does this show about scientific theories?

options.text: A theory becomes a fact once the evidence supports it
options.rationale: Strong support is treated as proof that closes the question for good.

options.text: New observations can change an accepted theory
options.rationale: Scientists use observations to arrive at theories, and a theory such as the Big Bang is developed further when new evidence, such as the supernova observations, arrives.

options.text: Theories about the distant past can never be tested
options.rationale: Events nobody witnessed are assumed to be beyond the reach of evidence.

options.text: The older theory must have been an untested idea
options.rationale: A revised theory is assumed to have had no evidence behind it in the first place.
